record.paper_title: Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid: status report, open problems, and outlook
record.original_question: How far can bootstrap algebraic multigrid techniques developed for non-elliptic and other challenging sparse systems be extended so that they become genuinely fast solvers for general sparse matrix equations beyond the problem classes where BAMG-like methods have already been implemented?

evidence.quote: Two important future research topics are thus to continue to investigate developing BAMG solvers for these and other non-elliptic problems and to determine how far these techniques can be extended as fast solvers for general sparse matrix equations.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Algebraic multigrid (AMG) is a class of iterative methods for solving large sparse linear systems $A x = b$, where $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is sparse, by building a hierarchy of progressively coarser linear systems together with intergrid transfer operators (interpolation $P$ and restriction $R$) and smoothers (e.g. Gauss–Seidel or weighted Jacobi), without explicit reference to an underlying geometric grid. A solver is called optimal (or a "fast solver") for a family of matrices $\{A_n\}$ of increasing size $n$ if it computes an approximate solution to $A_n x = b$ to a fixed relative accuracy in $O(n)$ arithmetic operations and storage, with convergence rate bounded independently of $n$.

Bootstrap AMG (BAMG) is a variant in which the interpolation operator and the coarse-variable set are constructed adaptively by simultaneously processing several test vectors that are improved by applying the current multigrid hierarchy, combined with a least-squares fitting procedure for the interpolation weights and, when needed, a multilevel eigensolver to expose slow-to-converge modes. BAMG-type methods have been demonstrated as fast solvers for various classes of sparse systems, including certain non-elliptic problems such as discretizations of the Dirac operator in lattice quantum chromodynamics, anisotropic and convection-dominated problems, and graph Laplacians.

Problem. Characterize the largest class $\mathcal{C}$ of families of sparse matrices $\{A_n\}$ for which a bootstrap algebraic multigrid method, in the sense above, can be designed to be a fast solver in the sense that:
(i) the setup cost is $O(n)$;
(ii) each multigrid cycle costs $O(n)$;
(iii) the asymptotic convergence factor is bounded above by some $\rho < 1$ independent of $n$.
In particular, determine whether BAMG techniques can be extended to yield fast solvers for general sparse matrix equations $A x = b$ beyond the problem classes (elliptic PDE discretizations, lattice Dirac systems, graph Laplacians, and related cases) for which they have already been realized, and identify structural conditions on $A$ (e.g. on its sparsity pattern, spectrum, near-null space, or associated bilinear form) that are necessary and/or sufficient for such an extension to exist.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is a broad open research direction concerning the extent of applicability of bootstrap algebraic multigrid. There is no general theorem establishing or refuting the existence of optimal BAMG-type solvers for arbitrary sparse systems; ongoing work continues to extend adaptive/bootstrap AMG to new non-elliptic classes (e.g. lattice QCD, Markov chains, graph problems), but no comprehensive characterization is known. The status is therefore open.
